utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, Douglas Stringer, Rachel Friedman, Thomas Laugel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic, Christopher Gosnell, and our intern, Mr. Alastair Livesey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stringer, I note the Defence wants to raise something but I would like to address, first, an issue with Mr. -- with the OTP. It's about the 92 ter transcript that was tendered yesterday without a redacted version. Is the redacted version in the meantime available? That's perhaps something I should have asked Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I believe it is. It was being redacted yesterday morning. My understanding was that there were just four parts from private session that had to be dealt with, and I believe that it's either completed or can be completed within the next hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to remind you of the Trial Chamber's order of 5 December 2012, where we asked the Prosecution to provide these on an ongoing basis before the witness comes or at least the moment the witness comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: There is a question if I could take a quick moment to raise in relation to this issue which I had intended to bring up. I think it's okay in public session. I think it was late last year we raised the -- the issue of public access to statements of Rule 92 witnesses because the statements were coming in at that time and this is why we are actually doing the public redacted versions now, to make more information available to the public. And I did get an inquiry from one of the media agencies that reports on this trial, and it may be that because we are marking the public redacted versions of the statements and actually putting them into evidence as exhibits, once they have got an exhibit label on them, Registry -- it may be the policy of the Chamber or the Registry in this case to just hold the exhibits and not make them fully available to members of the public to obtain. And of course I can see if there is a specific document or something, a photograph, but since it was our understanding that the public redacted versions of the statements were being done in order to provide greater access to the public, the question we were going to ask is whether the Chamber would either be acceptable to Registry making those available to the public or to the media if requested?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I know the problem and I see the problem. The question is when these statements or transcripts are made available and, indeed, it is the policy to make exhibits not publicly available before the end of the trial. And as you say, statements and those transcripts are considered as exhibits. I think the Registrar wants to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I wanted to say that we would have to look into it and see what our previous position was, because I -- I don't remember it exactly now, but the Registrar has obviously a better memory than I have. And, indeed, what we decided was that we would not on a general basis made these -- make these statements public, but that if there was a request for any statement or transcript of this kind in particular, we would look into it on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. President. I'll make sure that the people from the media and public who have been inquiring are made aware of the Chamber's position on this. If I could just raise one other unrelated thing. We did hear back from the Defence yesterday. This is in relation to the small correction to the transcript of yesterday's witness, Mr. Berghofer, from his testimony in the Mrksic case. The Trial Chamber will recall there was the audio -- in reviewing the statement, the audio revealed that there was a mistake it in the interpretation that appeared in the official transcript from that trial. The Defence has informed us that they agree, and so we will be sending this to CLSS asking that they make the adjustment in the official version of that transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zivanovic. Or Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We don't have very much to say in respect of this matter in terms of when -- the timing of the release of exhibits, including 92 ter statements. Your Honours understand our concern that producing a summary in court does potentially create a skewed impression of the testimony to which, of course, the Defence doesn't have an opportunity to respond in such a fashion. I would just say as an aside, of course, there is nothing stopping the Prosecution from, for example, redacting its witness summaries and making those available to the press. So if there is a need for the press to have further background on a particular witness, that would be a way that they could provide that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Was there anything else from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I thought you were just asking me about that particular issue. The matter that I wanted to raise with Your Honours was twofold. First - and I hope there would not be an objection from the Prosecution - is to make available to you in hard copy the two statements that we will be frequently referring to with the witness, and I propose also that she would have that in front of her in hard copy so she can turn back and forth as necessary. And the second request I would have is that we make a -- and I would make this proposal now. We will request Your Honours to admit both of these prior statements. And we've had discussions about prior statements in the past, and I entirely understand the Bench's position on this. But I would suggest this is an exceptional situation because we appear to have a witness on the stand who, I would suggest, is a sensitive witness or is vulnerable in certain ways, and what I would not like to do is toil through every inconsistency in these statements as compared to her testimony, which would be both laborious and potentially -- well, I don't want to use the word "traumatic," but naturally, Your Honours, I am not going to shy away from going into any important discrepancy, those that really must be put to the witness. But I really would not wish to tax this witness more than is necessary and I think we can avoid some of that simply by tendering the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, whereas your sensitivity to the witness's situation is understandable and what you propose on the face of it appears quite sensible, isn't there a problem -- isn't there an evidential problem that would remain insofar as that if you fail to challenge the witness on anything which on a reading is a clear discrepancy, it leaves the Chamber in a very difficult position in that the witness -- if these are admitted as exhibits, it leaves the Chamber in the position of not having had a -- the witness's explanation for what, on your eventual submissions would be a contradiction, an important contradiction. Do you see a practical way around that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I entirely agree that does pose some problem, but -- in respect of Rule 90(H), of course. I would suggest that Your Honours, however, are able -- in light of both the matters that I will put to her and the matters that I don't put to her able to assess that accordingly. Because -- and I've mentioned this before, there are many other judgements where precisely the concern that you've raised has arisen, and sometimes in respect of extremely important matters that were not put to the witness under Rule 90(H), and nevertheless, the Chamber assessed it in one way or another. Yes, probably lessening the extent to which there is impeachment value in the discrepancy. So I would suggest that that is what Your Honours could do when you are making that assessment. The other matter, the other aspect of this, if I may, is that the form of these documents is somewhat significant for your assessment as to whether or not they are a reliable record of what the witness said at the time. Just looking at the form of the 2000 statement, for example, seeing who was present, the fact that it was in her language, the nature of her attestation at the end, the nature of the attestation in the 2012 statement, I would suggest that these are all matters that really you would need to look at in full in order to understand what the impeachment value of these documents is. So on that basis as well, I would suggest that it's useful for Your Honours to have that in front of you. And again, Judge Hall, I entirely accept your point, but I would that if there is a problem in that regard, it can be discounted in your weighing of the testimony and of the impeachment value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, in response, if I can be heard on this. It's a broader issue. It's come up before and I'd like to address it. The Prosecution position has been, and although there are often reasons to consider cutting corners, the Prosecution's position is that statements of witnesses, written prior statements, are only admissible if the conditions - relevant conditions - for admission have been met under the Rules 92 ter, 92 bis, 92 quater. Now those conditions aren't being met here. In fact, as the witness told the Chamber yesterday, the 19 -- sorry, the early statement from 2000 made to the Croatian authorities is one that she didn't see. She signed it but she was very candid in telling the Chamber that she didn't review it, and she certainly didn't have an opportunity to make adjustments, to add other relevant points or to correct any mistakes in it. She hasn't adopted it. And so the Defence -- yes, it's a statement, it's got her signature, and it's appropriate for them to cross-examine the witness on it, but we're talking about impeaching a witness based on a statement that there is doubt about whether it's complete, whether it's fully accurate. That's number one. And so it's a bit unfair in a way to hold the witness to the statement and then use it as a basis for the next step, which is to compare it to a subsequent statement she made to an ICTY investigator many years later and then also to compare it to her testimony in these proceedings. It's about impeachment and about witness credibility and as appreciative we are of the Defence's sensitivity, we think that it's necessary in this situation not to cut corners but to actually do it the way that it is more appropriately done which is through cross-examination. There is another issue which is that if both statements come in, there is information in those statements that does not form a part of her direct evidence. There are some statements in there that the Prosecution finds somewhat useful, but they're not in evidence. And if the statements come in, the Chamber's going to be left trying to wonder with what are the inconsistencies that could have been raised on cross, as Judge Hall has just alluded to, but then there is a question whether the Chamber is going to be in a position to consider additional inculpatory statements made by the witness that are found in these statements as well. So that's another aspect, I think, that at the end in the final submissions the Chamber's going to be a little bit in the dark or it's going to have that additional element of uncertainty in terms of not only what could she have been impeached or asked about on cross but what else in here can we actually consider as evidence against the accused in the case? So, yes, it's a sensitive situation, the witness is -- well, we can see that she's emotional, and despite that, we think that it's necessary to do this the way it ought to be done, which is to put these to the witness on cross-examination, let her testimony and her responses be the evidence rather than the statements themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Just on the last point, Mr. President, which is a new element raised by the Prosecution in terms of whether or not once admitted these statements could be used for inculpatory purposes. The case law at the Tribunal is clear, that when a statement is tendered, a prior inconsistent statement is tendered in respect of -- to contradict the witness, to impeach the witness. That is the sole purpose of its admission and that is what we would suggest would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could just offer one last -- there is a reason why the Tribunal -- the Office of the Prosecutor does not accept and use witness statements prepared by domestic authorities as 92 ter statements, because of circumstances oftentimes in which those statements were made and taken by local authorities many years ago. The statements are a useful lead in locating witnesses, seeing in general what their evidence is, but the statements themselves aren't going to be the basis of -- solely the basis of the witness evidence and certainly is not going to be tendered into evidence as substantive evidence. That's why an ICTY statement is taken by an OTP investigator. This witness hasn't even affirmed the earlier statement, and it's being used now as -- the assumption from the Defence is it is her statement. Yes, she signed it, but she's told the Chamber that she wasn't given an opportunity to read it or to correct it, which, of course, are all procedures that are required for the admission of statements under our rules. So it's not even sufficient -- I mean, it's impeachment value is interesting but it's not established because the witness herself hasn't even -- it's not her statement certainly the way that we treat statements here in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I beg your indulgence just for one minor correction to what the Prosecution has said. In this very case - and I was very surprised to hear the Prosecutor say that they wouldn't rely to a national statement as meeting the minimum threshold for admissibility - in this very case they've tendered statements pursuant to 92 ter that came through -- that were based on national statements. And secondly, Your Honour, this statement is not -- it's not just this statement that comes out of blue. In 2012, the investigator went through chapter -- paragraph by paragraph, that statement with the witness, and the witness said paragraph 1 is true and correct; paragraph 2, the incident mentioned took place in 1971; paragraph 3 is true and correct, and so forth. So, in fact, the Prosecution tendered this 2012 statement pursuant to 92 ter in this very case, and only in the last ten days did we learn that they weren't going to tender it. So the notion that this doesn't meet the minimum reliability for impeachment, it doesn't seem consistent with their previous positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It would probably be unfair to the Defence to ask them to continue and finish their cross-examination without knowing the final decision that we would eventually take after more or less long deliberations. So then the most fair solution is, Mr. Gosnell, to deny your request and to have you organise your cross-examination in consequence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I appreciate that very much, Mr. President. Thank you. May I ask that we distribute the witness's prior statements. I have a copy for each member of the Bench. They are unmarked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I take it there is no objection from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And I have a copy in B/C/S for the witness of both statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, madam. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Madam, we apologise for the delay, the late start of the hearing. We had some administrative and procedural matters to deal with. And I remind you that you are still under oath. Mr. Gosnell, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Baranjek.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If I can just remind us where we left off yesterday, we were discussing the words that you heard Mr. Hadzic speaking into the radio transmitter. And what you testified yesterday was - and I'm quoting from page 3108 of the transcript: "Yes, he was shouting, laughing, he was shouting euphorically, 'Belgrade, Mladjo, send reservists over. Vukovar has fallen. I can head he had for Osijek tomorrow.'" Do you remember that that was your testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what I was asking you about at the end of yesterday was why it was your statement from the year 2000 to the Croatian police -- and by the way, madam, just to tell you, sitting in front of you, you have your two statements, those pieces of paper in front of you, you have your statement from the year 2000 and also --

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- your statement from the year 2012. In fact, looking at your desk, I can see that the statement on the right is the one from 2000 and the one on the left is the one from 2012. And if I could now ask you to just open your statement from 2000 -- the year 2000, and go to paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which one is number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you see that the paragraphs are numbered on your version there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I only have number 6. That's the last thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to bring me the statement that's now in the witness's possession. Well, actually, now we have just discovered that the original doesn't have numbering but apparently the translation does have numbering.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Madam -- and we're going to hand it back to you now, and it's on page 3 there, in the middle paragraph. And what you say there at page -- in this paragraph is: "At the time we were being registered, Goran Hadzic strutted into the room wearing camouflage uniform with an unbuttoned shirt with no rank or cap and approached a radio set and contacted Novi Sad, as far as I could hear. But the only thing I heard clearly was his words, 'We'll speak later. It's all right.'" Can you see that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: In the version we have it's on page 4, first paragraph on top of the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but that was just as I was entering the room. That's what he was saying over the radio set.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you recognise that what you said yesterday was significantly different from what you say here? In your testimony yesterday you say that he's shouting, he's apparently calling Belgrade, he's referring to an individual named Mladjo, he's talking about Vukovar having fallen, and then he's talking about sending reservists and going to Osijek. So my question is: Do you see that all of those elements are missing from your statement in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's because it wasn't written out fully. What you have written here as his words was something he was saying as I was entering the room. I had not yet been registered. It was later on that he contacted Belgrade, Mladjo, and then he called Braco to get vehicles. But this isn't recorded here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, in fact, I've looked through the rest of your statement in its entirety from the year 2000 and there is no mention of any of that. And feel free to take your time to look through, but do you see any mention of that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have reviewed the statement. I know what it says. But not everything has been written down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly that what you're saying is that during this interview with the police, you did mention these elements but they failed to write it down?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were many details that we were mentioning, all of us women who were being interviewed at the time. They were probably recording what they saw fit or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Ma'am, I don't think you've answered my question. Let me try to put it a different way. Do you remember whether you, during this interview, mentioned these additional details or, alternatively, it is that you didn't mention them and that is why they are not in the statement?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned more details than can be seen here. Not everything was recorded. And later on, I gave a statement like I am giving one today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: While you were giving this statement, were you -- was anyone in the room taking notes or were they typing? How was the statement actually recorded?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one policeman in plain clothes, an investigator. There was a lady and another gentleman. The lady was recording my statement, was noting it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was she noting it down with a pen or was she sitting at a typewriter or was she sitting at some other kind of transcribing or typing device, as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. She was noting it down with a pen. There were several of us women in the room, all those who were in that school. We were all being interviewed and she was using a ball-point pen to note it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how did it come about that you signed that document that you have in front of you? How did that occur?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They brought the papers over to us several days later to sign them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you read it before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did, but I didn't see that there were some flaws in there. There were some errors. And there was this other mistake that I made in mentioning the name of that man who turned out not to have been there, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you remember looking at this paragraph or this passage and saying to yourself, "Well, that's not quite what I said, but I'll sign it anyway"? Or is it that you looked at it, didn't notice it, and signed it thinking that in fact the statement was complete?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what was on my mind at the time. I didn't find it important. It didn't matter. In giving this statement, I was trying to find my husband. It wasn't my intention to accuse anyone or I don't know what. I was hoping that on the basis of this statement my husband would be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I can understand that, Madam Baranjek, and that's what makes it curious to my mind that 21 years after the events you can then recall a detail such as the name Mladjo being mentioned during this encounter. Is there any reason why you would remember that detail 21 years after the fact?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I remember many details of that night because what was uppermost in my mind was whether I and my children would survive that night, and that's why I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What was Mr. Hadzic wearing on this occasion? Can you describe a bit more fully what he was wearing.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wore a pair of camouflage trousers, they were a bit large. He was also wearing a shirt which was of a lighter colour than your normal camouflage shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was he wearing a jacket?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see a jacket in the school, but he must have worn it outside. It was cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you have any idea why, given that this was the 19th of November and Vukovar had effectively fallen the day before, and this information was known worldwide, why do you think -- do you have any information that could explain why Mr. Hadzic would be shouting into the phone to someone on the other end that Vukovar had fallen, send reservists?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, while we were in the shelter at Komerc, I didn't know that Vukovar had fallen the day before at all. We had no information, no radio, no TV. People said all sorts of things. In the morning we found out that we were supposed to go out. We heard it over the loud speaker, or what you call it, that we were being called out. We were being told to come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now in both your 2000 statement and then your statement in 2012, the first time you see Mr. Hadzic in both of these statements is in the room with the radio transmitters. And during your testimony yesterday, at pages 68 to 70 of the provisional transcript, you give a description of seeing Mr. Hadzic when you first arrive at the school in the hallway. Now, do you recall was it -- did you see Mr. Hadzic in the hallway upstairs or did you first see him down in the room with the radio transmitters?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that I saw him on a couple of occasions in the corridor and as I was passing by in the gym. That was all in passing. He kept moving about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You gave a very vivid description of his behaviour upstairs. You say that he was ordering -- that they were -- that he was basically being -- interrogating people, that he was shouting. He said that everyone should be questioned and whoever is not guilty would be allowed to go home. And then he told the milicija that they should get out and not interfere with his work. Now, Madam, I've looked at your statements, whether we're talking about upstairs in the hallway, downstairs in the room with the radio transmitters, after that, the next day, there is no description to be found in any of this -- in any of these events that accords with the description you gave yesterday. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that he was shouting in passing, telling his people to do their job, telling the police not to interfere with his job. I don't know whether anything -- everything should have been noted down. It's a pretty broad question that you've put to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, why don't you take your time and look at your statement from 2000 and look at your statement from 2012, and please tell us what indications there are in either of those statements of any of those rather specific recollections about Mr. Hadzic's behaviour.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that I reviewed the statement and that it did not record everything I said, and I remember vividly what happened that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in 2012, you sat down with a Prosecution investigator. You had your 2000 statement to hand. The purpose of that interview was precisely for you to supplement or correct your statement in any respects that you considered necessary, and you did do so in respect of a number of details, and yet there is no mention of Goran Hadzic at any time entering the building, telling the milicija to get out, interrogating people, shouting at people, issuing orders, none of that is mentioned in any of the sequences of events that you describe in your statements. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know how to explain this to you, but almost 22 years later I have no reason to lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When Mr. Hadzic -- when you first caught sight of Mr. Hadzic in the elementary school, did you instantly recognise him and say to yourself, "This is the man who was a close friend of my husband"? Correction, you've never said he was a close friend, "He is the man who was an acquaintance of my husband"?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I thought he would save my husband since he knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And your husband knew him because Mr. Hadzic shared a love of poetry with your husband and would visit your house where they would read poetry, look at paintings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And during your testimony yesterday, at page 61 of the provisional transcript, you said: "Mr. Hadzic came a few times to his studio and that's where we looked at paintings, read poetry." Do I understand from that when you say "we," that you were present during these visits and that you, along with Mr. Hadzic and your husband, read poetry and admired certain paintings?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I have the -- I'm looking at the transcript now, which has been updated. I understand Defence counsel is using yesterday's transcript. And it actually says: "Mr. Hadzic came a few times to the studio and that's where they looked at paintings, read poetry."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Perhaps on the basis of that correction I can just ask you: Did you ever join them?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever my husband was at the studio, I would step in, bring a cup of coffee or a glass of juice, whatever was needed, and went out. I was never there when he was with his friends, acquaintances, or customers in the studio.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Mr. Hadzic speaking or performing poetry?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't interested in that at all. I had my chores in the house. I can't say that I did hear him. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you know that your husband spoke to the director of Radio Vukovar and successfully managed to get Mr. Hadzic's poetry read on Radio Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that poetry on the radio yourself?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listened to the radio always, but I can't tell you that I was really interested in poetry. Nevertheless, it wasn't the -- it wasn't Mr. Hadzic himself who read poetry over the radio. It was the presenters working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you've sort of given an answer, but I would like to put question precisely to you: Did you hear Mr. Hadzic's -- or poetry being presented as Mr. Hadzic's being read on the radio?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever a poem was about to be read, they would always cite the author.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And so they would say, "This is a poem written by Goran Hadzic"?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The same applied to other authors, either poets or novelists or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did your husband tell you that Mr. Hadzic had ambitions to become better known as a poet?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. He did. He said that he had a lot of poetry, that he was interested in that. As for ambitions, I don't know about that. What I can tell you is that he loved poetry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did your husband -- did your husband tell you that Mr. Hadzic had any published collections of poetry?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly whether he published the book shortly afterwards or not. At any rate, poems were read over the radio. I really am not sure about when the book came out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you think there was a book of poems that did come out by Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was a book or -- or just a collection or what they call it. I think it was called a book of poems, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was there only one book or collection or were there -- was there more than one that you heard about from your husband?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Mr. Hadzic, if he had one or ten books published. I know about my husband who, by that time, had already had three books of poems published. Was it a book or just a -- in his case I don't know if the poems that were intended to be published were only just being put together or whether a book had already come out. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I know this is a difficult question, but if you could just search your memory and think back: Did you ever see any of these books or pamphlets or collections sitting around in your house or did perhaps your husband ever show you them?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never did see anything. I only saw my husband's books. As for the rest, the papers and documents that he had in his studio, I never went through them. I wasn't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Madam, I have to tell you I'm very perplexed by your description of Mr. Hadzic being a poet because as far as my information goes, he has never been a poet, never written poetry, never published poetry, never been a part of a poetry circle, never discussed poetry, sculpture, or painting with your husband. Is there any way that you could be -- and I'm sure that you're not fabricating all this. Is there any way that you could be confused about who it was who was coming and visiting your husband?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am not confused about the name or face. Whatever I said is something my husband had told me. I saw the man in my husband's atelier, studio.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 1D332, please, which is a -- it's on our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Mr. Gosnell. Witness, you have just said that you saw the man in your husband's studio. Who is the man? You were talking about Mr. Hadzic, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You had met him before the events that took place in Vukovar in your husband's studio; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I saw him for the first time when he arrived in the studio, although my husband had told me of him before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. That's very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could that be the man who you saw in your husband's studio who he told you was Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you know who this man is?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't. I don't remember either his first or last name or his face. I really don't remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we move the page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now this appears to be a -- some kind of an invitation or a pamphlet to a memorial of a poet in Pacetin. And I'm correct in saying that the man who you have described as Goran Hadzic was -- you were told by your husband that he was from Pacetin as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your husband told you that the man who was visiting your house and your husband's studio was from Pacetin; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 1D331, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That man in the white suit, is it possible that that is the man who was visiting your house and your studio and discussing poetry and art with your husband?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you know that this gentleman in the photograph worked with your husband at the Vukovar hospital?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps he did, but I don't know all of the people my husband worked with, including the doctors and nurses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Does the name Dr. Branko Kovacevic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't mean anything to me. I don't know. I don't remember him mentioning that man. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember your husband mentioning how many doctors in total there were at any given time at the Vukovar hospital between 1989 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: How many doctors there were in the hospital, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you whether your husband ever told you how many doctors there were in hospital.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't mention specific figures, but he did mention some of the doctors in conversations and I knew some of them. I don't see any reason why he would need to tell me the number of doctors in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, there were very few, correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. There may have been one, two, or five doctors per department. I never counted them. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm done with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Madam, I'd like to go back now to the chronology of events that you've described, and in your testimony yesterday - and working from the provisional transcript it's page 73 - there was a woman with red hair who brought you up from the radio room, the room with the transmitters, and back up to the hallway; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we went through the hallway to the classroom where the women and children were. That's where she took us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you were there guarded with about 20 other women by, as I understand it, a soldier from the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At first there was a JNA soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In your 2000 statement, you say -- you describe him as a gypsy. What do you mean when you describe him as a gypsy?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He looked like a Roma person. He was of dark complexion. In any case, his skin was darker than ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And while you were moving from the room with the radio transmitters and going to the classroom, what did you see, if anything?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other people in the hallway coming in from the bus and entering the building. A few of them were seated in the hallway. There was some people in camouflage uniforms, in civilian clothes, people moved up and down. In any case, there was a crowd.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what you say in your statement from 2000, and it's in the last sentence of paragraph 7, which is just above the paragraph -- and I know you don't have numbers paragraphs, madam, but it's above the paragraph that begins, "We stood in the corridor, in front of the stairs ..." And what you say is: "After the registration was over, that woman took us back up the stairs to the yard, and on the way I saw an open door on the right of the foyer through which I saw my husband, Ivan, standing at a microphone at the lectern in the sports hall, and behind him, the unavoidable grey-haired investigator." Now, first of all, this person described as the unavoidable grey-haired investigator, do I understand that that's the person who was wearing a white belt, which is the -- and a strap, a white strap and a white belt, and therefore in the uniform, as far as you knew, of the JNA military police?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the investigator who was present when my husband's house was searched back in 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in this paragraph, paragraph 7, you've just finished describing the words of Goran Hadzic into the transmitter. There is no mention here, is there, at all, of you seeing Goran Hadzic in the gym, is there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What I said is that he entered the gym, not that I saw him. I was not there. I was out in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you were able to see your husband in the gym.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the door was open and he stood so that I could see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you didn't see Mr. Hadzic there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him but I heard his voice. One could hear everything, although one couldn't see the entire gym. One could only see what was visible through the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So your testimony now is that you didn't see Mr. Hadzic but you heard his voice on that occasion; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When he drove the policeman and JNA members out of the gym, telling them they shouldn't meddle in his work. That's what I heard him say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, madam, this is the first time that you've ever said that you identify Mr. Hadzic in that gym on the basis of his voice.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He entered the gym and drove out the regular members of the army and the policemen, or there may have been several policemen. I didn't see him. I didn't see the policemen. But I did hear him say that they should leave and not meddle in his work. He told the people who were there, telling them, "You're all going to be interrogated, and if there is no blame on your part, you will be allowed to go home." Those were his words and I've already described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you didn't mention that in your 2000 statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In the statement you refer to, one cannot even find how many doctors there were in the hospital, and yet you asked me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So that's a no?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Repeat the question and I'll answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You didn't mention any of this, hearing Mr. Hadzic's voice issuing these many instructions, yelling, shouting, ordering people out, you didn't mention that in your 2000 statement? And in particular, in paragraph 7, where you're describing having looked into the gymnasium or the sports hall and having seen your husband.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw my husband and I saw Mr. Hadzic enter. Afterwards, I heard his voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, ma'am. That wasn't my question. But I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you could make your questions shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me ask you a different question. When you sat down with your statement in 2012, you had this paragraph in front of you. You were speaking with the investigator. You're making corrections. You didn't add any of these details, even though it's quite clear that during that interview the investigator was concerned to know about Mr. Hadzic's actions; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I said what happened. Perhaps not everything found its way into the statement. I don't know about that. You're asking me about some other details that I can provide. Perhaps not everything was written down. I said what happened in general terms, and now that you're putting these questions, I'm trying to explain everything that went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is it your view that you mentioned all of this during your interview with the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor and she didn't write it down, or is it your recollection that you didn't mention these things during that interview?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember which details I mentioned that may not have been noted down, but I know this for a fact: When you put a question to me, I tell you how things were. I don't know why some things were not put on paper. I really don't know. You asked me many things that are not even referred to on paper and I provided answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Ma'am, what I'm trying to understand is whether -- it's a simple question, it's whether you remember that you mentioned these things to the investigator and they were not written down or whether you didn't mention these things, you forgot them, you left them out because you viewed them as details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I object because this has been asked and answered in my view, not only through previous questions but her answer before was: "I really can't remember which details I mentioned that may not have been noted down." And I don't think there is any further assistance by asking her the question again and again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, with all due respect, it's precisely the ambiguity in that answer that's the problem, because it seems to give two different answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: The answer is that she -- just now: "I really can't remember which details I mentioned that may not have been noted down."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, note that that quotation seems to neither exclude that she didn't mention it or she maybe did mention it and it wasn't noted down. It seems that she's trying to say both and I really would like to, if possible, get a clear answer, and maybe that's not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you try to obtain that with one simple question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'll try to come at it from a different direction, Mr. President, and hopefully it will help.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Madam, you've used the word "details" a few times to describe Mr. Hadzic's behaviour that you've testified now before these Judges about. Is it possible that because you viewed them as details you didn't mention them? Well, let me put it to you a different way. Not that it's possible. Do you recall that you considered this behaviour of Mr. Hadzic to be a detail that you did not mention during your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You expect me to tell you something about the things that took a whole night and yet you want me to put it in a single sentence. I told you precisely how many times I saw Mr. Hadzic, where he went, what he said, what his behaviour was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At page 74 of yesterday's provisional transcript, and this, in our sequence of events, appears to be situated after your move to the classroom where you're detained by the JNA or guarded by the JNA officer whom you describe -- or soldier whom you describe as a gypsy. And the question that you were asked yesterday was: "Now, did you see Hadzic at any other point during your time in the elementary school?" And the answer was: "Yes, I saw him two or three more times. When he was passing through the corridor and entering the classroom where the questioning was taking place." Let me just stop there. What are you referring to when you say that he was entering the classroom where the questioning was taking place?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that his men were there in the classroom interrogating. Whoever was called out had to go there, separately, to be interrogated, both men and women. He would come out and probably issued orders. I don't know what he was doing inside but he kept going in and out. One could hear his voice while we were in the classroom, even though we were in a closed -- in an enclosed space. He was shouting at his men, telling them what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, here's what you say in your statement from 2000. And I'm leaving aside the issue of sequence or timing. Let's leave that aside. Let's leave that out of the issue. But what you say is this, that: "At some point the door was unlocked and a man with a large beard wearing an SMB --" and this is at paragraph 9 of the 2000 statement. "A man with a large beard, wearing an SNB uniform, entered the classroom and shouted at us: 'Right, Ustashas, and they are children.' "And he was followed by a young man of about 25 years old in civilian clothing, who I later learnt had come from Switzerland, who was carrying a folder with some papers in it, on which were our details and our husband's details. That young man called the women out one by one and took them for questioning upstairs." And then you describe that some of the women returned to the classroom where you were and you saw indications that they had been beaten. Now, madam, are you following your statement there where I'm reading?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't need to. I know it. I lived through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I've looked through all of your statement, both this statement and the statement from 2012, and what you say is that the classroom -- that these individuals were -- were taken upstairs. Do you remember that that's where the individuals were taken, the women who were with you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was only two or three steps up, one level up from where we were in the classroom. It wasn't all the way up on the upper floor but there were just a few steps, two or three, although I didn't count them precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And never before in any of your statements have you said, as you've just said now, that Goran Hadzic -- you could hear Goran Hadzic's voice during these interrogations.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could hear Goran Hadzic's voice as well as the voice of many others who passed by, including women. It's a school building with classrooms and one could hear everything, even in the hallway and out in the street voices can be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Ma'am, I've seen a photograph of the building. It's not small. It does have at least two storeys and a basement. You're saying you could hear everything in all parts of the building?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I was in all parts of the building. I was in the classroom. Not far away, where the women were, was another classroom where the people were being taken in to be beaten up and to be interrogated. I could hear that. I couldn't hear what was going on on the upper floor but one could hear the noise, people passing by, running, shouting. Of course one can hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why have you never before now mentioned that you could hear Goran Hadzic's voice during these interrogations?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. I have not. I told everything he said that I could hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You realise that you've never mentioned in any of your other statements even having seen Goran Hadzic in the corridor going anywhere?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that I saw him when the guard let us out to have a cigarette. I saw him pass by. I heard his voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, with the greatest respect, madam, that's not in your 2000 statement and nor did you make any correction to that in your 2012 statement.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you already that not everything was written down. When they put questions to me, I provided answers in as brief a way as possible. However, I always mentioned Mr. Hadzic, and I mentioned a number of corrections about people I didn't know whose names I only learned later. I don't know what you expect me to do now. To repeat everything that's on the paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I see the time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell. Thank you. Madam Baranjek, we take our first break. We'll come back at 11.00. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand I'm coming towards the end of my default allotted time. I would respectfully request that I be given some additional time. The witness's testimony is far more incriminating than initially foreseen, and given relative to the amount of time for the presentation of the direct examination, and even though it doesn't go to any specific paragraph in the indictment in terms of an event, it's obviously of some importance to Your Honours. So I would respectfully request an additional 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman, position on that request?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Only that to some extent the questions are being repeated. The witness is being asked the same thing repeatedly and so that should be borne in mind as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. How long do you think you will have in redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I think at this point probably within 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Your request is granted, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Madam, do I understand that it's your testimony that this young man from Switzerland was calling out names in the room where you were being held and that then those women whose names were being called were being taken upstairs and beaten; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The young man had a list and he read out the names. There was a lady in uniform who took the women to the room where they were questioned. Some of them came back beaten, others not, they didn't show any traces of beatings. And still others didn't even go up for questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So was this Swiss gentleman coming in and out of the classroom many times, a few times, just once? Do you remember how often he came into the classroom?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was with us in the classroom or outside of the classroom at all times. He was the one who came to guard us -- who replaced that other soldier. He came during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The night between the 19th and the 20th?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. It all started late in the evening. It may have been at 11.00 p.m. on the 19th, or at 1.00 a.m. of the 20th. At any rate, it lasted all through the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this gentleman from Switzerland, did he have any insignia or marks? Was he wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wearing some sort of uniform. I don't know which. It actually appeared to be a civilian-type of clothing because he didn't have any of the insignia. It was a bit multicoloured. At any rate, he had a list of all of us in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And was he of Swiss nationality or was he of Serbian nationality or some other nationality, as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was a Serb. He spoke to us and said that he had come to the village instead of his father, who had to stay behind in Switzerland because he was ill.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, I want to be absolutely fair with you about what's in your previous statements, and if I could just ask you now to direct your attention to paragraph 8 of your 2012 statement. What you say here is you describe the event where Mr. Hadzic comes into the classroom and speaks to you. And what you say in your 2012 statement was that after Mr. Hadzic calls out your name and asks about your husband's whereabouts, you say you didn't respond: "'He was here in the gym,' as is stated in my statement. Actually I told him, 'He was in the gym. You saw him.'" Now, is that an implicit reference to what you were describing earlier when you said that you looked into the gym and you could hear Mr. Hadzic's voice?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question again. I said that when he stepped into the classroom where the women and children were, he asked, "Who is Baranjek here," and I said it was me. And then he asked, "Where is your husband?" And I said, "You saw him in the gym." And I meant, you know, that place in the school, what you call it. And that was all the conversation we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in your 2000 statement, what you said instead of that was: "When he asked me where my husband was, I answered, 'He was there in the yard.'" That's at paragraph 9. Now, ma'am, I'm just trying to be fair to you, I'm not accusing you of any mistakes here, I'm just trying to understand. Are you saying that in your 2012 statement when you say that he was in the gym, you saw him, that was --

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. And when you say that: "Actually I told him he was in the gym. You saw him," were you referring to the moment when you were brought up from the transmitter room and taken to the classroom?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because that was the last time I saw him, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when Mr. Hadzic came into the room, did you say to him: "Mr. Hadzic, you're a good friend of my husband. Can you do anything to secure his release"?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday at page 75, you were describing events after this occasion when Mr. Hadzic enters the classroom, and you were asked the question by the Prosecutor: "And other than what you saw, is there anything else that you heard from the women with you about Hadzic's actions or what he said that night?" And your answer was: "Yes, there was a grandmother, an elderly woman who was sitting in the corridor. She said that -- in fact, all of us heard moans coming from that room." Now I just want to stop there and focus on that sentence, "in fact all of us heard moans coming from that room." When was that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the night. There weren't as many people in the hallway or in the corridor. People were already put up in the various classrooms or in the gym. We were in the classrooms and, of course, we could hear moans. You hear moaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At paragraph 8 of your statement from 2000 - and in this respect, you made no correction when you were speaking to the investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor in 2012 - this is what you said: "On 20 November 1991, immediately after 0030 hours" -- and, ma'am, if you want to follow along, this is mid-way through paragraph 8 of your statement in 2000, and it's the paragraph that begins: "We stood in the corridor in front of the stairs ..." And at about mid-way down in that paragraph what you say is as follows: "On 20 November 1991, immediately after 0030 hours, I heard someone approach the guard and insist that he unlock the door for them with the words, 'Unlock the door so we can slaughter the Ustashas,' to which the soldier responded, 'Can't be done, pal. Orders." "At about 0200 hours, Zorana Vitic and I asked the soldier for permission to go to the toilet and have a cigarette. And the gypsy soldier, who we found out was from Vaska -- Vajska, told us that we could smoke a cigarette in front of the door. Since around that time until dawn, since I was next to the door to the corridor, I heard people screaming and yelling, the sound of shots from firearms and of celebrations and of cars stopping. And I would like to say that the shooting was an expression of happiness in the celebration and that all these sounds came from outside the building in my estimation." Now that's your description in your statement of -- in the year 2000. You made no correction to that in 2012. No indication there, is there, that you heard moans or the sounds of beating inside the school, is there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement in 2012 was there to supplement the one that I gave before. I don't see what it is that you want me to do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All I'm putting to you, and I'm not asking you to do anything in particular except to look at your statements, and taking both statements together --

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know exactly what I stated and I stand by that, word for word. Now, there is something on one piece of paper but it isn't on the other. I don't see what it is that you want. Do you want every single thing that happened during that night to be there on paper? Why am I here, then? So what do you want me to do? Do you want me to just repeat what is there on paper without adding a single word? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor, when you met her in 2012, suggest that it was not important to be complete, especially in respect of your testimony about Mr. Hadzic or about violent actions going on at the school?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement that I gave earlier was read out to me. I was asked about it and I said immediately that I had corrections to make, that this was not the man's name, that this isn't the way it happened, and that's what I said. I did it that way. I don't understand what it is that you mean now. Do you want everything that happened that night to fit into these two papers? What of my emotions? What of the emotions and feelings of my children? Those are nowhere to be found on these papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did the grandmother who informed you about the fate of your husband, did she tell you that while you were at the school?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have an opportunity to talk to her about the school. I didn't even know that she had seen anything. It was in Zagreb when we met after a while, in a hotel. I did know that she was seated in the corridor. I did see her. She was an elderly woman. And then that's when she told me. I think that it was in mid-1992 that she told me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Madam, I'm obliged under the rules of this Tribunal to put to you very clearly what our position is, and our position is that Mr. Hadzic was at no time at the Borovo Elementary School on 19 or 20 November 1991.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. There were very many people in the school and I wasn't the only one to have seen him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You're testifying as a public witness. Obviously people know that you're here. Has anyone spoken to you about your testimony before coming here other than representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who you mean. My girlfriends who were with me in the school know that I am testifying. I don't know who else you mean. My children? Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Has any public official from Croatia contacted you about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody contacted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The same would be true there was no public official from Serbia who contacted you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you say, and I ask you this as a very general question, would you say that there are very strong negative feelings about Mr. Hadzic amongst public opinion in Croatia today?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what, I talked to my girlfriends about Mr. Hadzic, as I've just said. Generally I'm not interested in politics, and believe me when I tell you that I don't watch the news. I only am interested in knowing what the weather forecast is. I have no interest in having him either convicted or acquitted. My husband is not here anymore, so...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Ma'am, if I could just ask for one additional clarification or detail. If you can recall, you've told us how Mr. Hadzic was dressed on the 19th. Do you remember how he was dressed on the 20th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you how many times I saw him. The last time was, I believe, past midnight on the 20th, but I'm not sure, when he went down the corridor. I think he was dressed the same way. I don't know, really. I just saw him go by. I don't think he had anything else on him. I saw him only -- I only saw his back and heard his voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, ma'am. I'm not referring to that. What I'm referring to, and your statements are very clear in this regard, although your testimony here has not been equally unequivocal, but in your previous statements you make clear, and I refer you to paragraph 9 of your 2000 statement, which in this regard was not corrected in your 2012 statement, where you say that Goran Hadzic entered the classroom at 10.00 in the morning and that would be the 20th of November. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he entered the classroom where we, the women and children, were? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was dressed the same way as he was when I saw him down there by radio sets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Madam Witness, thank you for your patience and your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm renewing the application to admit the two prior statements. We can wait until after the redirect, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that a request for reconsideration, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I -- I suppose I -- I wasn't sure whether your previous ruling was actually a final ruling or whether you were merely giving me guidance as to how I should conduct my cross-examination given that time was short and it would be best to proceed, of course. So -- but if Your Honours do consider it to be a final ruling, then, yes, I would request reconsideration. I'm not sure ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will proceed first with re-examination, if that is what you intended rather than discussing the issue of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Unless you want to answer or intervene in Mr. Gosnell's request, I was expecting you to start re-examination, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Baranjek, I have some questions first about your husband and Mr. Hadzic's association before the day in Borovo Selo, when they discussed poetry and so forth. Did your husband think that Mr. Hadzic was a talented poet?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did he think he had a future in writing poetry?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't believe that. But he appreciated when people were into poetry and dealing with it, so he didn't mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Why did he -- why do you believe he helped him have his poetry read on the radio?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, because he appreciated the fact that there were other people who loved poetry like he did, and also because the poetry of all sorts of people was read on the radio, and he was glad about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did you happen to -- did Hadzic continue to come to your husband's studio up until the eruption of the conflict in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. This was before.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when he stopped coming?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all happened before 1990. Not later. He wasn't coming later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: When you -- when was it that you first learned that he had become involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was stories circulating in the town, people were saying these things, and that was the sort of time before the war. So it was from what other people were saying, that was 1990, early 1991, the Log Revolution, when it started. That's how we called it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you and your husband ever discuss between you that the man who had been coming to his studio was now involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, at that time I didn't hear anything about Mr. Hadzic from my husband because he was talking about the things that were happening in the hospital. There wasn't much said about Mr. Hadzic. It was more the case that people in the street, neighbours, and those who knew him talked about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Was -- when you saw him in the Borovo Selo school, was that the first time you had seen him in a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I may have seen him previously on TV. I don't remember. Perhaps yes, perhaps no. But I did hear that they had uniforms, people were talking.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now when Mr. -- I just want to read to you something that the Presiding Judge asked you yesterday and your answer. The question was: "Ms. Baranjek, I would like to ask you one follow-up question. You told us that Mr. Hadzic, I think at three different moments, in the gym, in the classroom, in the room where the radio transmitters were, asked for your husband, where he was. Do you know --" Well, I'll pause there for a moment. Now, on one of those occasions, in the classroom, you testified that he read out your name from the list. He asked, "Ms. Baranjek." In the other -- I wanted to know if on the other two occasions he also referred to you by name?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Do you believe that in the school he recognised you from the earlier period when he knew your husband?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't recognise me. It was probably because of the list and because of the fact that my husband was in the gym. He probably saw the list of women and children before entering the classroom. That's why asked who -- whose last name was Baranjek, who was the person.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Do you know if he found -- found your husband at some point?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection, this goes beyond the scope of the cross, unless I have some indication otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I would just ask for some latitude in that regard, given that it follows up on that she didn't know why he was looking for him, so the follow-up is whether she knows if he found him after being in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Gosnell is right, Ms. Friedman. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Well, do you know if Hadzic found out that your husband had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Same objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps just a follow-up to that answer that she did not know why he was looking for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether he did want to help him?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Same objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think you better leave it, Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I will leave it here. I think it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Just one final question. Ms. Baranjek, did you hear any -- are you aware of an article being published prior to Mr. Hadzic coming to The Hague where it describes his encounter with his mother and it says that he recited a poem to her or it was reported that he recited a poem to her. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. I have no disclosure of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I understand perfectly well that it's not being tendered, but it at least ought to have foundation for the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes. It can be tendered. This arises directly out of cross. My learned friend put to the witness that he had no information of Mr. Hadzic even liking poetry and I -- the article is not yet translated. It's in B/C/S. I will seek to tender it after. For now, that is the basis on which I am asking the witness if she knew of the report that he read the poem, not written by himself, mind you, by a Russian poet, but if she had read that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You want to say something before we rule, Ms. Friedman? I don't know. I may ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Just that we will be able to have the original article uploaded shortly if that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Objection overruled. You may ask the question, Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Baranjek, were you aware of this article or of any news reports about Mr. Hadzic reading poetry to his mother?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said already that I don't know about it. And I don't watch the news, either. I learned of Mr. Hadzic's arrest from my daughter only a few days later. There is really nothing I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Baranjek.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask Your Honours just for one moment. Yes. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Baranjek, this brings an end to your testimony. We know how difficult this is for you and we thank you very much for coming to The Hague and assist the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness. We wish you a safe journey home. The Court Usher will escort you out of the court. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, your request is pending, your request about the two statements, the tendering of the two statements, we will come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you like any submissions on this now or would you prefer something in writing or would you prefer no further submissions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Submissions in writing would perhaps be -- would not be a bad idea, Mr. Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I suppose there is no other witness, Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: No, there is no other witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 4th day of March, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.40 a.m.,
